finding.headline: At 54, you are now in the 50-and-over catch-up group for 401(k) and IRA limits.
details: For 2027, the 401(k) catch-up limit for people aged 50 and over is $8,500, so you can contribute up to $34,000 a year in a 401(k).
The IRA limit stays at $7,500 for 2027, and the IRA catch-up for people aged 50 and over stays at $1,100.
At age 60 to 63, a higher 401(k) catch-up limit of $11,750 applies, which may be worth planning for in the years before you retire at 65.

finding.headline: About 21% of your income goes to tax now, and retirement tax looks very low.
details: Of your $136,000 gross pay, about $28,000 goes to federal, state and payroll tax, leaving about $108,002 after tax.
All of your savings now sit in taxable and cash accounts, so 100% of withdrawals come from there first. Your plan shows $5,106 a year drawn, with about $843 of tax per year in retirement.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Check with a tax professional before you move money between accounts.

finding.headline: This household has no children, college, or pet costs to plan for.
details: Your basic living costs once retired are about $30,800 a year, or $2,567 a month. Health costs before Medicare, at 65, are about $10,000 a year.
Your mortgage ends in 2028, and costs fall by about $12,900 a year when it does. Your debts total $55,200 today, with about $12,900 a year in payments and $5,394 a year in interest.
Long-term nursing home care costs about $129,575 a year, and it often lasts about 3 years. The plan does not include this cost.

finding.headline: The full spending goal lasts in 37 of 100 market scenarios; basics are paid in all 100.
details: The plan kept is a simple plan: stocks at 110 minus your age, with Social Security claimed at age 69. Markets are uncertain, so these results are not promises.

Spending about $52,300 a year is safe in 90 of 100 scenarios. That is below your $56,000 goal, a gap of $3,700 a year. Your savings are $16,900 now, and the median at retirement is $189,000, with a median of $0 at age 96.
Your 10,100 credit card balance at 27% costs about $2,688 a year in interest, so paying it down first would help. Your emergency fund also covers only 2 months, short of the 3-month target by $7,925.

finding.headline: You can count on $52,300 a year: $30,800 for basics and $21,500 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $30,800 a year.
Your spending goal of $56,000 a year lasts in 37 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Until you retire you save about $12,902 a year: $12,902 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $50,900 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 69 for each of you, which pays about $59,000 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $33,900 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 96. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
